[[Image:UCSB-NobelBanner-WalterKohn.png|thumb|280px|right|A banner on a lightpole at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]], commemorating Walter Kohn being awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1998.]]

'''Walter Kohn''' ({{IPA|de|ˈvaltɐ ˈkoːn}}; March 9, 1923 – April 19, 2016) was an Austrian-American [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]] and [[theoretical chemistry|theoretical chemist]]. He was awarded, with [[John Pople]], the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] in 1998.<ref>[http://www.auslandsdienst.at/press/archive/austriaculture_1999.html From Exile to Excellence] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110531200733/http://www.auslandsdienst.at/press/archive/austriaculture_1999.html |date=May 31, 2011 }}, by Karin Hanta (Austria Culture Vol. 9 No. January 1/February 1999)</ref> The award recognized their contributions to   understanding the electronic properties of materials. In particular, Kohn played the leading role in the development of [[density functional theory]], which made it possible to calculate [[quantum mechanical]] electronic structure by equations involving the [[electronic density]] (rather than the many-body [[wavefunction]]). This computational simplification led to more accurate calculations on complex systems as well as many new insights, and it has become an essential tool for materials science, condensed-phase physics, and the chemical physics of atoms and molecules.<ref name="Sham2016">{{cite journal|last1=Sham|first1=Lu J.|author-link1=Lu Jeu Sham|title=Walter Kohn (1923–2016) Condensed-matter physicist who revolutionized quantum chemistry|journal=Nature|volume=534|issue=7605|year=2016|pages=38|pmid=27251269|doi=10.1038/534038a|bibcode=2016Natur.534...38S|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Early years in Canada==
Kohn arrived in [[England]] as part of the [[Kindertransport]] rescue operation immediately after the [[Anschluss|annexation]] of [[Austria]] by [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/walter-kohn-onetime-refugee-who-became-nobel-laureate-in-chemistry-dies-at-93/2016/04/24/77b6f896-08c0-11e6-bdcb-0133da18418d_story.html|title=Walter Kohn, onetime refugee who became Nobel laureate in chemistry, dies at 93|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=April 25, 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160531065252/https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/walter-kohn-onetime-refugee-who-became-nobel-laureate-in-chemistry-dies-at-93/2016/04/24/77b6f896-08c0-11e6-bdcb-0133da18418d_story.html|archive-date=May 31, 2016}}</ref> He was from a [[Jewish]] family, and has written, "My feelings towards Austria, my native land, are – and will remain – very painful. They are dominated by my vivid recollections of 1 1/2 years as a Jewish boy under the [[Nazi]] regime, and by the subsequent murder of my parents, Salomon and Gittel Kohn, of other relatives and several teachers, during the [[Holocaust]]. ... I want to mention that I have a strong Jewish identity and – over the years – have been involved in several Jewish projects, such as the establishment of a strong program of Judaic Studies at the University of California, San Diego.".<ref name="auto">{{cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1998/kohn-bio.html |title=Walter Kohn – Biographical |publisher=Nobel Prize Organization |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170613104215/http://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1998/kohn-bio.html |archive-date=June 13, 2017 }}</ref><ref name="Sham2016"/> Kohn also has identified as [[Deist]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Top Scientists On God: Who Believes, Who Doesn't|url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/max-tegmark/angry-atheists_b_2716134.html|work=The Huffington Post|access-date=May 13, 2013|quote=I am very much a scientist, and so I naturally have thought about religion also through the eyes of a scientist. When I do that, I see religion not denominationally, but in a more, let us say, deistic sense. I have been influenced in my thinking by the writing of Einstein who has made remarks to the effect that when he contemplated the world he sensed an underlying Force much greater than any human force. I feel very much the same. There is a sense of awe, a sense of reverence, and a sense of great mystery.|first=Max|last=Tegmark|date=February 19, 2013|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130226053646/http://www.huffingtonpost.com/max-tegmark/angry-atheists_b_2716134.html|archive-date=February 26, 2013}}</ref>

Because he was an Austrian national, he was transferred to [[Canada]] in July 1940 after the outbreak of [[World War II]]. As a 17-year-old, Kohn traveled as part of a British convoy moving through U-boat-infested waters to [[Quebec City]] in Canada; and from there, by train, to a camp in [[Trois-Rivières]]. He was at first held in detention in a camp near [[Sherbrooke]], [[Quebec]]. This camp, as well as others, provided a small number of educational facilities that Kohn used to the fullest, and he finally succeeded in entering the University of Toronto. As a German national, the future Nobel Laureate in Chemistry was not allowed to enter the chemistry building, so he opted for physics and mathematics.<ref name="auto"/>

==Scientific career==
Kohn received a war-time bachelor's degree in applied mathematics at the end of his one-year army service, having completed only 2½ out of the 4-year undergraduate program, from [[University College, Toronto|University College]] at the [[University of Toronto]] in 1945; he was awarded an M.A. degree in applied mathematics by Toronto in 1946. Kohn was awarded a Ph.D. degree in physics by [[Harvard University]] in 1948, where he worked under [[Julian Schwinger]] on the three-body scattering problem. At Harvard, he also fell under the influence of [[John Hasbrouck Van Vleck|J. H. Van Vleck]] and developed an interest in solid-state physics.

He moved from Harvard to [[Carnegie Mellon University]] from 1950 to 1960, after a short stint in Copenhagen as a [[National Research Council of Canada]] post-doctoral fellow. At Carnegie Mellon, he did much of his seminal work on multiple-scattering band-structure work, now known as the KKR method. His association with [[Bell Labs]] got him involved with semiconductor physics and produced a long and fruitful collaboration with [[Joaquin Mazdak Luttinger|Luttinger]] (including, for example, development of the [[Luttinger-Kohn model]] of semiconductor [[band structure]]). In 1960 he moved to the newly founded [[University of California, San Diego]], held a term as the physics department chair,<ref>[http://www.physics.ucsb.edu/~kohn/ UCSB Physics Department Website] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100619060159/http://www.physics.ucsb.edu/%7Ekohn/ |date=June 19, 2010 }} 'W. Kohn, BIOGRAPHICAL DETAILS'</ref> and remained until 1979. It was during this period, he, along with his student [[Chanchal Kumar Majumdar]] developed the ''Kohn–Majumdar theorem'' related to [[Fermi gas]] and its bound and unbound states.<ref name="Chanchal Kumar Majumdar (1938–2000) – An obituary">{{Cite web |url=http://www.iisc.ernet.in/currsci/jul102000/book%20reviews.pdf |title=Chanchal Kumar Majumdar (1938–2000) – An obituary |date=July 2000 |publisher=Current Science |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060717183439/http://www.iisc.ernet.in/currsci/jul102000/book%20reviews.pdf |archive-date=July 17, 2006 }}</ref><ref name="SchefflerWeinberger2011">{{cite book|author1=Matthias Scheffler|author2=Peter Weinberger|title=Walter Kohn: Personal Stories and Anecdotes Told by Friends and Collaborators|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wl_vCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA264|date=June 28, 2011|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-642-55609-8|pages=264–}}</ref> He then accepted the founding director's position at the new [[Institute for Theoretical Physics (Santa Barbara)|Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in Santa Barbara. He took his position as a professor in the [[UC Santa Barbara Physics Department|Physics Department]] at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] in 1984; where he worked until the end of his life.

Kohn made significant contributions to semiconductor physics, which led to his award of the [[Buckley Prize|Oliver E. Buckley Prize]] by the [[American Physical Society]]. He was also awarded the Feenburg medal for his contributions to the [[many-body problem]].
His work on density functional theory was initiated during a visit to the {{lang|fr|[[École Normale Supérieure]]}} in Paris, with [[Pierre Hohenberg]], and was prompted by a consideration of alloy theory. The
[[Hohenberg–Kohn theorem]] was further developed, in collaboration with [[Lu Jeu Sham]], to produce the [[Kohn–Sham equations|Kohn-Sham equations]]. The latter is the standard workhorse of modern materials science,<ref name="dft">E. K. U. Gross and R. M. Dreizler, ''Density Functional Theory'', Plenum 1993</ref> and even used in quantum theories of plasmas.<ref name="dft" />
In 2004, a study of all citations to the ''Physical Review''&nbsp; journals from 1893 until 2003, found Kohn to be an author of five of the 100 papers with the "highest citation impact", including the first two.<ref>Redner, S. ''Citation Statistics From More Than a Century of Physical Review''&nbsp; 2004 {{cite arXiv |eprint=physics/0407137 |last1=Redner |first1=S |title=Citation Statistics from More Than a Century of Physical Review |year=2004 }}</ref>
[[File:Walter Kohn Oxford University.JPG|thumb|Walter Kohn receiving an [[honorary doctorate]] at [[The University of Oxford]]]]

In 1957, he relinquished his Canadian citizenship and became a [[naturalized citizen]] of the [[United States]].

In 1963 Kohn became a Member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], a Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1969, and a member of the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 1994.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Walter Kohn|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/walter-kohn|access-date=January 26, 2022|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Walter Kohn|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/walter-kohn-ckmytu/|access-date=January 26, 2022|website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Walter+Kohn&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=January 26, 2022|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> In 2011, he became an honorary member of the [[Austrian Academy of Sciences]] (ÖAW). He was also a Member of the [[International Academy of Quantum Molecular Science]].

==Death==
Kohn died from jaw cancer at his home in [[Santa Barbara, California]], on April 19, 2016, at the age of 93.<ref>{{cite web |title=Memos &#124; Office of the Chancellor |url=https://chancellor.ucsb.edu/memos/?4.20.2016.Sad.News...Professor.Walter.Kohn |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160513093916/https://chancellor.ucsb.edu/memos/?4.20.2016.Sad.News...Professor.Walter.Kohn |archive-date=May 13, 2016 |access-date=April 21, 2016 |website=University of California, Santa Barbara}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Pernett |first=Stephanie |date=April 22, 2016 |title=UCSB Professor and Nobel Laureate Walter Kohn Passes Away at 93 |url=http://dailynexus.com/2016-04-22/ucsb-professor-and-nobel-laureate-walter-kohn-passes-away-at-93/ |newspaper=[[Daily Nexus]] |location=[[Santa Barbara, California]] |access-date=April 22, 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160423125411/http://dailynexus.com/2016-04-22/ucsb-professor-and-nobel-laureate-walter-kohn-passes-away-at-93/ |archive-date=April 23, 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/04/26/science/walter-kohn-nobel-winning-scientist-dies-at-93.html?_r=0|title=Walter Kohn, Nobel-Winning Scientist, Dies at 93|publisher=The [[New York Times]].com|access-date=April 25, 2016|date=April 25, 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160430084341/http://www.nytimes.com/2016/04/26/science/walter-kohn-nobel-winning-scientist-dies-at-93.html?_r=0|archive-date=April 30, 2016}}</ref><ref name="Sham2016"/>
